item.title: TorchNeuron Model Support Space Shows Which Transformers Run on AWS Trainium
item.description:
TorchNeuron Model Support Space Shows Which Transformers Run on AWS Trainium

🔍 Overview

A new Hugging Face Space, torch‑neuronx‑model‑support, lets you see whether a given Transformers model runs unmodified on AWS Trainium and provides the exact script to run it yourself.

🛠️ How it works

  • Uses the torch‑neuronx package, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium.
  • Runs Transformers models on Trainium the same way they run on any other device.
  • The provided run.py script loads the model with from_pretrained, shards it when needed, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

📊 What the Space displays

  • PASS/FAIL result for each model.
  • Number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over.
  • Wall‑time of the run (compilation included).
  • Peak device memory usage.
  • The Neuron stack version, required packages, and the run.py script used.
  • If a model is omitted, the Space explains why (e.g., not prioritized or truly incompatible).

📈 Testing methodology

  • Tests run on a Trainium2 (trn2) instance, typically in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container.
  • Each model is sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights (maximum 16 cores, i.e., four Trainium2 devices).
  • Most models use tensor parallelism; Mixture‑of‑Experts models without a tensor‑parallel plan use expert parallelism only.
  • The test generates 32 tokens and checks them.
    • On a single core, the tokens are compared with a CPU run of the same checkpoint.
    • When sharded, a small judge model verifies that the text is fluent English.
  • A PASS only confirms correctness of the 32‑token output; it says nothing about throughput or longer generations.

⚙️ Configurability

  • The Space opens on the Selected view (our own selection of top‑downloaded and trending models).
  • You can switch to Trending or Downloads views and type part of a model name to look it up.
  • Versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx‑cc) and Transformers library can be chosen.
  • When a model is left out on purpose, the Space tells you the reason.

📌 Current scope

  • Only Transformers models are tested.
  • The selection is limited to text‑generation and image‑text‑to‑text models.
  • Only models that fit on four Trainium2 devices (up to 16 cores) are included.

🚀 Getting started

  1. Open the Space (it starts on the Selected view).
  2. Choose the desired neuronx‑cc and Transformers versions.
  3. Follow the displayed run.py script: install the listed packages, then run on a trn2 instance.
  4. The first run compiles the model’s graphs; subsequent runs can reuse compiled graphs by copying them from the public NEFF cache bucket.

🔎 Where the data comes from

  • All rows are sourced from the public aws‑neuron/torch‑neuronx‑model‑support dataset.
  • The dataset contains one Parquet file per pair of neuronx‑cc and library versions.
  • Each row stores the model’s result, any error, the stack versions, and the run.py script that was executed.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

#TorchNeuron #AWS #Trainium #Transformers #ModelSupport

Source: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

item.title: Training Qwen3 on a Single AWS Trainium2 Instance with TorchNeuron and NKI MoE
item.description:
Training Qwen3 on a Single AWS Trainium2 Instance with TorchNeuron and NKI MoE

This post demonstrates three ways to train the Qwen‑3 model on a single AWS trn2.48xlarge instance equipped with Trainium2 accelerators, using TorchNeuron, torchtitan‑neuron and optional NKI mixture‑of‑experts kernels.

🔍 Overview

  • TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device, enabling torchtitan to use it through standard PyTorch interfaces.
  • When torch_neuronx is installed, TorchNeuron registers the Trainium device and torchtitan detects it at startup.
  • The walkthrough runs on a single trn2.48xlarge instance (16 Trainium2 accelerators, 128 physical NeuronCores, 64 logical NeuronCores at LNC=2).

⚙️ Environment

Component Version
torch 2.14.0
torch_neuronx 2.14.3
transformers 5.16.0
torchtitan‑neuron release‑2.33 (0.2.2+neuron.1)
Instance trn2.48xlarge (16 Trainium2, 128 physical NeuronCores, 64 logical NeuronCores)

🚀 Training Configurations

1️⃣ Transformers v5 backend

  • Uses AutoModelForCausalLM to load Hub models and reads/writes published safetensors.
  • Launches 64 training processes, one per logical NeuronCore.
  • Data‑parallel sharding across all 64 ranks.
  • Saves final checkpoint as Hugging Face safetensors.
  • Example result for Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507:
    • Step‑1 loss 6.54 from published weights.
    • Step‑1 loss 12.43 from random initialization.

2️⃣ torchtitan native Qwen3Model

  • Switches to torchtitan’s native implementation by changing config.model_spec.
  • model_registry("4B", attn_backend="sdpa") selects the native Qwen3 model with scaled dot‑product attention (SDPA).

3️⃣ NKI Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) kernels

  • Adds Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) MoE kernels from the torchtitan‑neuron recipes.
  • Uses torchtitan’s override registry to attach the custom kernel.
  • qwen3_nki_moe_config() replaces the MoE block with the NKI grouped‑experts implementation, selects SDPA and a gather‑free rotary embedding.
  • Configuration details:
    • Data‑parallel sharding across 64 ranks, tensor‑parallel degree 1.
    • num_experts=64 sets the number of experts (not the expert‑parallel degree).
    • CompileConfig(enable=False) runs the example in eager mode.
  • TorchNeuron supports the registered NKI operators in both eager execution and torch.compile modes.

🧩 Execution Modes

  • Eager mode: Neuron compiles operations as they execute.
  • torch.compile: Neuron compiles the captured graph.

📚 Getting Started

  • Use a single trn2.48xlarge with either the AWS Deep Learning AMI for Neuron or a Neuron PyTorch training container.
  • Install torch_neuronx to enable device registration and torchtitan detection.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Demonstrates that a single Trainium2‑powered instance can train a 4‑billion‑parameter LLM using standard PyTorch interfaces.
  • Shows flexibility: the same hardware can run a Hugging Face Transformers backend, a native torchtitan implementation, or custom NKI MoE kernels without changing the underlying instance.
  • Provides a reproducible recipe for researchers and engineers to explore performance trade‑offs between eager execution, graph compilation, and custom kernel extensions.

#Trainium #TorchNeuron #Qwen3 #MoE #Neuron

Source: Train Qwen3 on AWS Trainium with torchtitan | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Systematically Analyzing Inference Performance on AWS Trainium with TorchNeuron
item.description:
Systematically Analyzing Inference Performance on AWS Trainium with TorchNeuron

A new guide provides a walkthrough for ML practitioners to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where time is spent during model execution, starting from scratch with no prior profiling experience.

🧩 How it works

The profiling process utilizes AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron integrates with PyTorch via the PrivateUse1 extension point, allowing the accelerator to integrate without adding a dedicated dispatch key like cuda. The torch_neuronx package registers Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code.

TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows with minimal code changes, including:

  • Eager execution
  • torch.compile
  • Standard PyTorch APIs
  • Integration with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for custom operators and performance optimization

⚙️ Key details

Profiling is managed through torch.profiler.profile using a NeuronConfig passed as experimental_config.

Parameter Function
modes Selects data streams to capture, such as runtime traces and device instructions
capture_enabled_for_nc Selects the NeuronCores to trace
correlate_device_time=True Propagates device time into the key_averages() table to compare CPU and Neuron device time

To ensure accuracy, torch.neuron.synchronize() must be called inside the profiler loop; otherwise, the profiler may export before the device finishes, leaving the Neuron time column empty. The recommended schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls to record one warm iteration without initial setup overhead.

🔍 Analysis and Output

After profiling, the output directory contains system traces and, if device data was captured, paired files identified by a numeric hash:

  • NEFF (Neuron Executable File Format): Contains the compiled Neuron executable.
  • NTFF: Contains the hardware instruction trace.

Users can analyze these results using Neuron Explorer, a browser-based viewer for the device timeline, system trace, and per-engine breakdown, accessible via a Visual Studio Code extension or SSH tunnel.

As a practical example, the walkthrough compares a naive RMSNorm (using individual PyTorch operations like multiply, mean, add, reciprocal square root, and multiply) against torch.rms_norm(), which is lowered to a single fused Neuron kernel.

#AWSTrainium #TorchNeuron #PyTorch #MLprofiling #InferencePerformance

Source: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
